paper_title: Design of Experiments (DoE) and Process Optimization. A Review of Recent Publications
mechanistic_insights: Design of Experiments (DoE) is a powerful tool for process optimization, superior to the traditional 'one factor at a time' (OFAT) approach because it can uncover interactions between variables.

The DoE workflow involves defining objectives, factors/variables and their ranges, and responses, followed by selecting an experimental design, performing reactions, analyzing data, and confirming the results.
Screening designs are used to identify the most important factors, while optimization designs (e.g., Response Surface Methodology - RSM) are used to find the optimal conditions for those factors.
DoE is central to the Quality by Design (QbD) approach in pharmaceutical development, helping to define the 'design space' and 'proven acceptable ranges' (PARs) for critical process parameters.
Technological advances, such as parallel reactors and high-throughput screening, have made the implementation of DoE more practical in process chemistry.

quantitative_outcomes.best_performing_conditions: This is a review paper and does not present a single set of best-performing conditions. It summarizes numerous examples, such as a Heck coupling optimized to 99% yield by exploring temperature (90-120 °C), dilution (5-10 mL), and reaction time (8-24 h).
quantitative_outcomes.notes: This paper is a comprehensive review of the application of Design of Experiments (DoE) in chemical process optimization, drawing examples from publications in Organic Process Research & Development from 2003-2013. It does not present new experimental data but rather illustrates the power and methodology of DoE across a wide range of reaction types, including hydrolysis, acylations, oxidations, and metal-catalyzed cross-couplings. The primary focus is on the statistical methodology for process improvement, not on a specific chemical transformation.
